# Shiyi Peng’s Post

Shiyi Peng

1w

Yesterday our Y Combinator group voted us into the top 9 🎉 and we got to demo for everyone. In round 1, my cofounder Jerry created an agent for his own strategy on AnyAlpha , live in front of everyone, and we gave it $100. Then we went to dinner. the agent went to work. By the time we got back up to demo for the whole group, it had already made $53. The whole room was watching it execute in real time. Such a fun moment. Super excited about how much agents can do now. Build something people want.🧡 Build something agents want.🧡 (Yes, we want all agents created on AnyAlpha to have access to the best data, run on the most reliable infra, and eventually generate alpha for their owners: our users!)

# InstaCloud Migrates AnyAlpha to Autoscaling Containers

Hang Huang

2w

We just did our first Collison install for InstaCloud! Shiyi Peng and AnyAlpha (YC F26) are building an app that lets users build, backtest, and track their own sports models. Being in the current Y Combinator batch, they need to move fast. AWS was too tedious for them: Managing DevOps and scaling, picking t-shirt sized EC2 instances, and paying for unused compute were big pain points. So we met with them in-person to migrate their app to InstaCloud! Now with autoscaling containers, they can spend more time now building AnyAlpha and growing their awesome product. Excited to see what Shirley and the team build next! ☁️

  * Noah Ispas

2w

Most teams have adopted Kubernetes. The thinking behind it, they haven't. I spent years in cloud native, including the CNCF and SIG work. The pattern repeated every time. The cluster is running. Deployments are still manual. Environments still drift. Nobody is sure what is actually in production. Declarative over imperative. Infrastructure as code. Reproducibility by default. Those are the parts that change how a team works. Those are the parts that get skipped, because a running cluster looks like the finish line. The change arrives when the team stops working around the infrastructure and starts trusting it. #PlatformEngineering #DeveloperExperience #Kubernetes #CloudNative

A routine deploy can scale your AWS ECS service down from 20 tasks to 2 during peak traffic, with no warning. The cause is how CloudFormation/CDK updates a stack. It compares your new template with the last deployed template, not with what is actually running. If DesiredCount is in the template, it is applied on every deploy that updates the service. In a CDK app that is almost every deploy, because a new container image creates a new task definition revision.

At The Context Company (YC F25), we’re hyper-optimizing for developer experience. Today, we open-sourced a free, local-first observability tool for AI agents. It shows every generation, every tool call, and every failure in real time, right inside your local dev environment. No cloud, no sign-up, no dashboard. - Runs fully locally - 7 lines of code to set up - Completely open source Optimizing AI agents is very fun, but debugging them and understanding exactly what they do is annoying lol. While Arman was building agents at Mintlify and I was working on Gmail Intelligence at Google, we kept hitting the same problem: agents fail silently. They get stuck in loops, pick the wrong tools, and hallucinate - and digging through logs to figure out why is awful. Instead of scattering console.log() everywhere or inspecting hundreds of objects in the console, we wanted a small local-first solution that simply shows what happened as it happened. So we built it. Repo: https://lnkd.in/enqg3uT7 Docs: https://lnkd.in/epEuMJzU And one more thing: We also quietly turned on self-serve onboarding for our full platform, with a generous free tier. If you want observability not just locally, but in staging and production, you can sign up and start in minutes. We’re building The Context Company for developers who care about reliability. If that’s you, would love your feedback.

A huge thank you to Cerebral Valley, La Maison and the RAISE team for an unforgettable hackathon.
